draft.body:
On October 6, 2026, OpenAI announced a collection of 377 mathematical results, highlighted by an automated proof claiming to settle the quasi-Riemann hypothesis—a weaker formulation of the Riemann hypothesis, long considered one of the foremost open questions in mathematics. Stanford University mathematician Jared Duker Lichtman described the development as "the most significant AI-for-math achievement so far, by quite a margin," according to reporting from [Quanta Magazine](https://www.quantamagazine.org/ai-proved-the-quasi-riemann-hypothesis-what-happens-now-20261019/). While the full Riemann hypothesis remains an open Millennium Prize Problem after more than 160 years, resolving the quasi-Riemann hypothesis provides fixed mathematical limits that directly govern the distribution of prime numbers.

Techniques used within the proof relied in part on earlier methods pioneered by Maksym Radziwiłł of New York University and Alexander Dunn of the Georgia Institute of Technology. Radziwiłł noted that the consequences of establishing the quasi-Riemann hypothesis are "staggering," adding that "in a sense, the vast majority of consequences of RH already follow from quasi-RH." Rather than inventing new foundational concepts, the system linked known analytic tools in an unexpected order. "The proof is a surprising synthesis of well-known ideas," Dunn told [Quanta Magazine](https://www.quantamagazine.org/ai-proved-the-quasi-riemann-hypothesis-what-happens-now-20261019/).

[[FIG1]]

## The Mathematical Scope of the 7/8 Boundary

The classical Riemann hypothesis, conjectured by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, concerns the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function, denoted ζ(s). Riemann demonstrated that any nontrivial zeros must lie inside a critical strip where the input's real part sits between 0 and 1. The original hypothesis posits that all nontrivial zeros sit precisely on the vertical critical line where the real part equals 1/2. Numerical calculations have confirmed that the first 12 trillion nontrivial zeros lie on this line, but an analytic proof covering all zeros has remained elusive. In 1896, mathematicians proved that zeros could not reside on the extreme edges of the strip, confirming the prime number theorem. As Enrico Bombieri noted in documentation for the Clay Mathematics Institute, any failure of the hypothesis would create havoc in the distribution of prime numbers.

The quasi-Riemann hypothesis requires establishing a strictly narrower exclusion strip rather than locating zeros exclusively on the 1/2 line. As detailed by [Binary Verse AI](https://binaryverseai.com/quasi-riemann-hypothesis/), OpenAI's primary manuscript, dated September 30, 2026, claims a fixed zero-free half-plane for any input where the real part strictly exceeds 7/8. Using the functional-equation symmetry of the zeta function, ruling out zeros with a real part above 7/8 simultaneously rules out zeros with a real part below 1/8. This confines all nontrivial zeros to the closed strip between 1/8 and 7/8.

Crucially, this boundary is uniform across infinite height. Classical analytic results already establish zero-free corridors near 1, but those corridors shrink as the imaginary coordinate increases. The new proof provides a barrier of fixed width that holds regardless of height. Beyond the Riemann zeta function, the paper claims the identical 7/8 boundary applies to all Dirichlet L-functions and finite-order Hecke L-functions over the number field ℚ(√−3), as documented by [Binary Verse AI](https://binaryverseai.com/quasi-riemann-hypothesis/).

## Two Papers, Lean Verification, and Prose Shortcomings

OpenAI released two versions of the argument within its mathematics release, cataloged under family 003 among 722 manuscripts spanning 372 families. The primary manuscript runs 199 pages and proves the 7/8 boundary with formalization in the Lean interactive theorem prover. The second manuscript, completed roughly a week later, presents a weaker boundary between 1/12 and 11/12 across 49 pages. This shorter version received human editing for readability but has not been formally verified.

Despite the mathematical milestone, human researchers noted severe stylistic problems in the machine-generated text. Radziwiłł stated in an email to [Quanta Magazine](https://www.quantamagazine.org/ai-proved-the-quasi-riemann-hypothesis-what-happens-now-20261019/) that both documents "are horribly written (in a way that would lead to immediate rejection at any mathematical journal)" and fall far short of the expository standards expected in analytic number theory. Because of this density, mathematicians have concentrated their review on the 49-page paper, whose brevity makes the underlying architecture easier to deconstruct.

[[FIG2]]

The Lean verification materials for the 199-page paper target a zeta nonvanishing theorem and Dirichlet L-function nonvanishing assertions, allowing three standard logical axioms: propositional extensionality, quotient soundness, and classical choice, according to [Binary Verse AI](https://binaryverseai.com/quasi-riemann-hypothesis/). The accompanying repository includes a Comparator challenge framework that allows outside researchers to evaluate the machine-checked argument against defined criteria.

## Anatomy of the Proof and Prime Number Consequences

The architecture of the proof operates in two sequential stages. According to technical documentation summarized by [Binary Verse AI](https://binaryverseai.com/quasi-riemann-hypothesis/), both stages examine character sums through two distinct mathematical representations: direct bounds and Poisson summation connecting the construction to the reciprocal of a target L-function. Because a vanishing function creates a singularity in its reciprocal, proving that the reciprocal extends holomorphically across a domain rules out zeros.

The initial stage establishes the 11/12 boundary using completed cubic-theta sums, a reflection identity, and large-sieve estimates to control aggregate term sizes across families of arithmetic terms. The second stage sharpens the boundary to 7/8 by modifying arithmetic sums with selected prime factors to cancel local contributions, alongside unequal averaging scales and moment estimates that secure positive savings in the exponents.

Establishing the 7/8 bound yields direct consequences for prime numbers. Because zeta zeros govern error terms when estimating the count of primes up to a given number, a uniform bound of 7/8 supports power-saving prime-counting error estimates. It also rules out exceptional real Landau–Siegel zeros in the interval between 7/8 and 1. In addition, the manuscript provides a polylogarithmic bound on the least quadratic nonresidue modulo an odd prime, yielding a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for finding modular square roots.

## Model Attribution and Scrutiny

OpenAI attributed the proofs to an unreleased internal frontier model rather than a publicly deployed ChatGPT system. Production records note that work on the zeta zero-free region was an exception to the team's standard automated procedures, and published reasoning traces did not disclose discovery paths for family 003, as reported by [Binary Verse AI](https://binaryverseai.com/quasi-riemann-hypothesis/).

The theorem provides no algorithm for breaking modern integer-factoring cryptography, nor does it resolve the full Riemann hypothesis. Number theorists continue to inspect both the Lean code and the prose proofs discussed in [Quanta Magazine](https://www.quantamagazine.org/ai-proved-the-quasi-riemann-hypothesis-what-happens-now-20261019/) to confirm that the full mathematical interpretation survives rigorous scrutiny.

faq.q: Did AI solve the Riemann hypothesis?
faq.a: No. The full Riemann hypothesis remains an open Millennium Prize Problem. OpenAI claimed its system proved the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, establishing that nontrivial zeros must lie in a strip between 1/8 and 7/8 rather than proving they all lie on the 1/2 line.

faq.q: Which AI model generated the proof?
faq.a: OpenAI attributed the result to an unreleased internal frontier model, not a publicly available consumer ChatGPT model.

faq.q: Has the mathematical proof been verified?
faq.a: The 199-page manuscript establishing the 7/8 boundary was formalized and verified in the Lean interactive theorem prover with a Comparator verification framework. The shorter 49-page paper establishing an 11/12 boundary was human-edited but has not been formally verified in Lean.

faq.q: What concrete mathematical consequences follow from the proof?
faq.a: The proof supports power-saving error terms in prime-counting estimates, rules out Landau-Siegel zeros in the interval (7/8, 1), and provides a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for finding modular square roots.
